findings.body: Replacing `loadMany(ids)` with an awaited `load(id)` inside the loop turns a single batched fetch into one repository round-trip per id. That makes latency and backend load grow with input size and can regress heavily on large lists.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function now performs N sequential repository calls instead of one batched call, increasing end-to-end latency and potentially exhausting the repo's connection pool or rate limits.

findings.body: Interpolating `userName` into a shell command lets attacker-controlled input alter the command line. A username containing spaces or shell metacharacters can execute an unintended command or change the report arguments; pass arguments directly to the child-process API instead of building a shell string.
findings.failure_scenario: If `userName` comes from untrusted input, a value like `alice; rm -rf /` is executed by the shell when `execSync` runs, resulting in arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid shell command injection in report invocation

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` drops the first element from every successful result, so callers no longer receive the full report output. For a single-row report this now returns an empty array, which is a visible correctness regression.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"])` runs, it returns `["second"]` instead of the original rows, and a one-row report becomes empty.
findings.title: Preserve the first report row instead of slicing it off

findings.body: This test only checks that the result is truthy, so it no longer verifies the spec requirement that rendering preserve every input row. The new implementation could drop rows and still pass.
findings.title: Assert that renderReport preserves the full row list

findings.body: Passing the user name through `sh -c` makes the command line shell-interpreted, so any metacharacters in `user` can alter the command being run instead of just being an argument to `report`. The previous direct `Command::new("report")` call did not have this injection surface.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` contains shell syntax such as `alice; rm -rf /`, `sh -c` will execute the extra command instead of calling `report` with a literal user argument, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid invoking the report command through the shell

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` is undefined behavior for `UserRecord` unless it is a very specific plain-old-data type, and even then it can still produce invalid values that poison the subsequent `merge` call. This can turn a normal `fetch_user` invocation into memory corruption or intermittent crashes.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `fetch_user` on a build where `UserRecord` is not fully valid in an uninitialized state can trigger undefined behavior, leading to corrupted records or process crashes when `UserRecord::merge` reads the scratch value.
findings.title: Remove the use of `std::mem::uninitialized()` here

findings.body: Interpolating `user` into a shell command and passing it through `sh -c` allows shell metacharacters in the username to be interpreted as additional commands. This turns a normal report render into a command-injection sink if the username can ever be influenced by an attacker.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker supplies a username like `alice; rm -rf /`, `sh -c` executes the extra command instead of just invoking `report`, leading to arbitrary command execution on the host.
findings.title: Avoid building a shell command from `user`

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` removes the first element on every successful call, which contradicts the stated intent to preserve report rows and also throws on empty input. The previous behavior returned the original list unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When the report produces zero rows, `sublist(1)` raises a range error; when it produces one or more rows, the first row is silently lost from the result.
findings.title: Return the full row list instead of dropping the first item

findings.body: Building a shell command with `user` and executing it through `sh -c` reintroduces shell parsing, so metacharacters in a user name can change the command that runs. The previous `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` avoided this by passing the value as an argument.
findings.failure_scenario: If a user name contains spaces, quotes, or shell metacharacters, the shell will reinterpret them and may execute an unexpected command instead of the intended report invocation.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argv element instead of via `sh -c`

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: This assertion no longer verifies the function's behavior: `isNotNull` passes even if `renderReport` drops rows, reorders them, or returns the wrong data. The test should still check the exact output so regressions in the new row-slicing logic are caught.
findings.failure_scenario: If `renderReport` starts returning the wrong rows, this test still passes because any non-null list satisfies `isNotNull`, so the regression reaches release unnoticed.
findings.title: Keep the report test asserting the returned rows content

findings.body: This changes the previous bulk `loadMany` call into one `load` call per id, and each call is awaited before the next starts. For larger input lists, the total latency becomes the sum of all individual round trips and can significantly slow down requests or exhaust worker capacity under load.
findings.failure_scenario: When a caller passes hundreds of ids, the loop performs hundreds of sequential repository fetches instead of one bulk read, causing request latency and throughput to degrade sharply.
findings.title: Avoid loading items serially in the enrichment loop

findings.body: This changes a previously batched `loadMany` call into one `load(id)` await per element, so the cost now scales with the number of ids and will amplify latency under larger inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function performs one repository round-trip per id instead of a single batched fetch, causing much slower enrichment and avoidable load on the backing store.
findings.title: Batch repository lookups instead of loading one id at a time

findings.body: This replaces a direct `ProcessBuilder` invocation with `/bin/sh -c`, which reintroduces shell parsing and argument expansion. A username containing spaces, quotes, or shell metacharacters can change the command that gets executed, violating the requirement to pass user names as process arguments without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name like `alice; rm -rf /` is interpolated into the shell command and executed by `/bin/sh`, causing the report process to run unintended commands instead of just receiving the user name argument.
findings.title: Pass the report command as arguments without a shell

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` always removes the first element, so the method no longer preserves the report rows it receives. It also throws on empty input because the start index is greater than the end index.
findings.failure_scenario: When `render` is called with `[]`, `subList(1, 0)` throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`; when called with any non-empty list, the first row is silently lost from the result.
findings.title: Return the original rows instead of dropping the first entry

findings.body: This test no longer verifies the service contract. `assertNotNull(...)` passes even if `render` drops elements, reorders rows, or returns the wrong subset, so the current change can regress unnoticed.
findings.failure_scenario: If `render` starts returning the wrong rows (for example, dropping the first element as the new implementation does), this test still passes and the regression ships.
findings.title: Assert the rendered rows instead of only non-null

findings.body: Changing `fetch` from `User fetch(String, Integer)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String, int)` breaks the stated compatibility goal: existing callers compiled against the old return type and nullable timeout argument will no longer match this signature. If the intent is to preserve caller compatibility, this API change needs an overload or to retain the original method shape.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that was built against the previous `fetch(String, Integer)` contract will fail to compile or link after upgrading, because the method now requires a primitive `int` and returns a different type.
findings.suggestion: User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs) { return new User(id, timeoutMs == null ? 30000 : timeoutMs); }
findings.title: Keep the `fetch` contract compatible with existing callers

findings.title: Avoid invoking the shell with untrusted user input

findings.body: Slicing with `rows[1:]` removes the first element from every non-empty input, so rendering no longer preserves every row as required. The previous behavior returned the original slice unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains data like `[]string{"first", "second"}`, the caller receives only `[]string{"second"}`, causing the first row to disappear from the rendered report.
findings.title: Return the full row set instead of dropping the first row

findings.body: This workflow now runs in the `pull_request_target` context and explicitly checks out the PR head SHA before executing `npm test`, so the test process runs attacker-controlled code with access to `RELEASE_TOKEN`. A malicious PR can print or exfiltrate that secret from the CI job.
findings.failure_scenario: When an external contributor opens a PR, their modified test or build script runs under `pull_request_target` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` available, allowing the token to be stolen from the workflow logs or sent to an external server.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN to code from the pull request

findings.body: Switching this workflow to `pull_request_target` while still checking out the pull request head and passing `RELEASE_TOKEN` into `npm test` means code from forks can execute with a repository secret available in its environment. findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a PR that edits the test script to print or send `RELEASE_TOKEN`; the workflow checks out that PR commit and runs it with the secret exposed, leaking the repository token.

findings.body: Building a shell command string here reintroduces shell interpretation of `user_name`, which the spec explicitly forbids. If a username contains spaces or shell metacharacters, the command can be misparsed or exploited, and the behavior now diverges from the required argument-vector execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A username like `alice; rm -rf /` is passed through `shell=True`, so the shell interprets it as multiple commands and can execute unintended actions instead of invoking `report` with one username argument.
findings.title: Keep using an argument vector instead of shell=True

findings.body: Slicing off the first element drops data from every successful render, which contradicts the requirement to preserve every input row in order. Any caller expecting the original report rows will now silently lose the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is `['first', 'second']`, the function returns only `['second']`, so the rendered report is missing its first line.
findings.title: Preserve the full row list when returning the rendered report

findings.body: Passing a formatted string to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` makes `user_name` part of a shell command. If the username contains shell metacharacters, the command can execute unintended extra shell syntax instead of just invoking `report` for that user.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user_name` contains characters like `;` or `$(...)`, the shell interprets them during `subprocess.run`, which can run arbitrary commands or alter the report invocation.
findings.title: Avoid constructing the shell command from user input

findings.body: This test no longer checks the function's actual output, so it would still pass if `render_report` drops or reorders data. That weakens coverage for the behavior this change affects.
findings.title: Restore an assertion on the returned rows

expected.label: replacement test no longer checks row preservation

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: This change makes `timeoutMs` required and changes the return value from an object to a 2-tuple. Any existing caller that relied on the previous default argument or on `result.id` / `result.timeoutMs` will break at runtime when this exported function is upgraded.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does `fetchUser("123")` or reads `fetchUser("123").timeoutMs` will now either pass an extra argument everywhere or receive a tuple instead of an object, causing `undefined` property accesses and downstream failures.
findings.title: Preserve the existing `fetchUser` contract

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: Changing the return value from an object to a two-element tuple removes the `id`, `timeoutMs`, and `fetchedAt` object properties that existing code is likely reading. That is an incompatible API change rather than a compatibility-preserving refactor.
findings.failure_scenario: Code that does `fetchUser(id).fetchedAt` or reads `timeoutMs` from the returned object will now get `undefined` because the function returns an array instead of the previous record.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Keep the original return shape for existing consumers

findings.body: Building a command string with `${userName}` and passing it to `execSync` runs the report through a shell, which violates the requirement that report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell. Any user name containing shell metacharacters can alter the command that gets executed.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller passes a user name like `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell interprets the injected separator and executes unintended commands instead of only running the report.
findings.title: Avoid interpolating the user name into a shell command

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` removes the first element on every call, so the function no longer preserves the report rows it was given. That changes the output for all non-empty inputs and can silently lose data.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is `['first', 'second']`, the function returns only `['second']`, so callers lose the initial row from every report.
findings.title: Return the full row set instead of dropping the first entry

findings.body: `execSync` runs the interpolated string through a shell, so `userName` can alter the command instead of being passed as data. This creates a command-injection path that did not exist with `spawnSync(..., ["--user", userName])`.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker can supply `userName` like `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes the extra payload when `renderReport` runs, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid building the shell command from user input

findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does `const user = fetchUser(123);` and then reads `user.timeoutMs` will now see `undefined` (or destructure the wrong value), causing downstream logic that depends on the timeout and timestamp fields to fail.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs: timeoutMs ?? 30000, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Preserve the public return shape of fetchUser

findings.body: Removing the default makes `timeoutMs` `undefined` for existing callers that only pass `id`, which changes the function's behavior and breaks the current call contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously invoked `fetchUser(123)` now receives `undefined` for `timeoutMs` instead of the existing 30000 default, so downstream code that expects a numeric timeout can misbehave or fail.
findings.title: Preserve the default timeout parameter

findings.body: Building a shell command string and passing it through `sh -c` reintroduces shell parsing for `user`, so metacharacters in the username can alter the command line instead of being passed as a single argument. findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` produces a value without running its constructor and is undefined behavior for types that are not plain old data. If `UserRecord` contains any invalid bit patterns, references, or heap-owning fields, this can cause immediate memory corruption or later crashes when `UserRecord::merge` reads or drops it.
findings.failure_scenario: When `fetch_user` is called, the uninitialized `UserRecord` can contain invalid bytes; `UserRecord::merge` then reads or drops that value, triggering undefined behavior such as memory corruption or a process crash.
findings.title: Avoid creating `UserRecord` with `mem::uninitialized`

findings.body: The path is validated with `canonicalize()` and `strip_prefix()`, but the final `File::open(candidate)` re-resolves the pathname. findings.body: This change replaces a single bulk repository call with one `Load` invocation per ID. If `Repository.LoadMany` was batching database or network access, the new loop introduces an N+1 pattern that can significantly increase latency and load for large `ids` slices.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, `Enrich` now performs one repository round-trip per item instead of one batched fetch, causing slow requests and extra backend pressure.
findings.suggestion: func Enrich(ids []int64, repo Repository) []Item { return repo.LoadMany(ids) }
findings.title: Avoid per-ID loads when a batch loader already exists

findings.body: This loop now performs one `repo.Load` call per id, so if `Load` hits storage or a remote service the work becomes N+1 and scales poorly with input size. The previous implementation used `LoadMany`, which could fetch the items in a single batch.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many elements, the function issues one backend round-trip per id, increasing latency and potentially overloading the repository or connection pool.
findings.title: Batch the repository lookup instead of loading each id separately

findings.body: This change breaks caller compatibility by changing both the parameter type and the return type. Code built against the previous `FetchUser(id string, timeout *time.Duration) User` contract will no longer compile, which contradicts the stated goal of preserving compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compiled against the old API passes a `*time.Duration` and expects a `User`; after this change the call no longer matches the function signature, causing a compile-time break across every existing consumer.
findings.suggestion: func FetchUser(id string, timeout *time.Duration) User { return User{ID: id} }
findings.title: Preserve the original FetchUser signature

findings.body: `io/ioutil` has been deprecated for file operations since Go 1.16. Using the modern `os.ReadFile` keeps the code on the supported API surface and avoids carrying a deprecated import forward.

findings.title: Replace `ioutil` with `os` for file reads

findings.body: `pull_request_target` executes this workflow with the repository's secrets and write-scoped token, but the checkout is pinned to the PR head SHA and the subsequent `npm test` step runs that untrusted code. A forked PR can therefore execute arbitrary commands with `RELEASE_TOKEN` available and exfiltrate it or perform other privileged actions.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a malicious forked PR; the workflow checks out their commit and runs `npm test` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment, allowing the PR code to steal the secret or abuse repository privileges.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted PR code in a `pull_request_target` workflow

findings.body: This workflow now runs `npm test` on the pull request's head commit while injecting `RELEASE_TOKEN` into the job environment. On `pull_request_target`, a forked PR can change the test script or any code executed during tests to read and exfiltrate that secret.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a malicious fork PR that edits the test runner; when the workflow executes, the PR code reads `RELEASE_TOKEN` from the environment and sends it to an attacker.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: This workflow now depends on `actions/labeler@v6`, which is a moving tag. If the upstream action is compromised or publishes a breaking change, the labeler job will pick it up automatically. Pinning to a full commit SHA limits that supply-chain risk.
findings.failure_scenario: If the `v6` tag is retargeted or a release is compromised, the workflow will execute attacker-controlled action code on future pull requests and can modify labels with repository write permission.
findings.title: Pin GitHub Actions to a commit SHA

findings.body: Switching this job from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` gives it the base repository token and makes the later `actions/labeler` step run with write access on untrusted fork PRs. That is a materially different security model than a clean-context workflow and can let a compromised action version mutate PR metadata.
findings.failure_scenario: When a contributor opens a pull request from a fork, the workflow now executes with write-capable PR credentials; if any step is compromised or misused, it can alter labels on the target repository instead of running read-only.
findings.title: Avoid running the workflow in pull_request_target context

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.

findings.body: Building a shell command from `user_name` and executing it with `shell=True` reintroduces shell interpretation of the argument. Any user value containing metacharacters will be parsed by the shell rather than passed as a single argument, which can lead to command injection or broken execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A username like `alice; rm -rf /` is interpolated into the command string and executed by the shell, causing unintended commands to run instead of just calling `report` with one argument.
findings.title: Pass argv to subprocess.run instead of invoking a shell

findings.body: Slicing off `rows[1:]` changes the function contract by discarding the first input row. The specification requires rendering to preserve every input row in order, so this silently loses data whenever the caller passes a non-empty list.
findings.failure_scenario: When the caller passes `['first', 'second']`, the function returns only `['second']`, so the rendered report omits the first row and the output no longer matches the input order/content.
findings.title: Preserve all rows instead of dropping the first entry

findings.body: This test only asserts that the function returns a non-`None` value, so it would pass even if rows are dropped or reordered. The spec explicitly requires preserving every input row in order, so the test no longer verifies the behavior that matters.
findings.title: Restore a test that checks row preservation

findings.body: Building a shell command string and running it with `shell=True` makes the call vulnerable to shell metacharacters in `user_name` and changes argument parsing semantics. The previous form passed the username as a single argv element, which is both safer and more predictable.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user_name` contains spaces, quotes, or shell metacharacters, the spawned process may receive the wrong argument or execute unintended shell syntax, leading to command injection or broken report generation.
findings.title: Pass argv directly instead of invoking a shell

findings.failure_scenario: A caller doing `fetch_user(...)["id"]` or `json.dumps(fetch_user(...))` will start receiving tuple behavior instead of a dict payload, causing runtime errors or response-format regressions.
findings.title: Preserve the dictionary return shape expected by callers

findings.body: `PurePath(...).name` discards every path segment except the last one, so any identifier containing a slash or backslash is silently rewritten before the lookup. That can make valid users unresolvable or, worse, resolve the wrong record if two IDs share the same trailing segment.
findings.failure_scenario: When a caller passes an ID such as `org/alice`, the query runs with `alice` instead of the original key and returns the wrong row or no row at all.
findings.title: Preserve the full user ID when querying

findings.body: Returning `rows.slice(1)` removes the first input row, which directly contradicts the requirement that rendering preserve every input row in order. Any report with at least one row will now lose data in the rendered output.

findings.body: Interpolating `userName` into a shell command and passing it to `execSync` lets attacker-controlled input change the command that gets executed. A username containing shell metacharacters can run arbitrary commands instead of just invoking `report` with one argument.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker can supply `userName` like `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes the injected command when `renderReport` runs, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Prevent shell command injection in report invocation

findings.body: Slicing the returned array removes the first input row, so rendering no longer preserves every row as required. Any caller with a non-empty first row will observe missing data in the output.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is `['first', 'second']`, the function now returns `['second']`, so the first rendered row disappears from the report.
findings.title: Return the full rows array instead of dropping the first row

findings.body: Interpolating `userName` into a shell string allows shell metacharacters in the name to alter the command that gets executed. A crafted username could run arbitrary commands instead of just invoking `report` for that user.
findings.failure_scenario: If `userName` contains characters like `;` or `&&`, `execSync(command)` will execute the injected shell fragment and the process can run attacker-controlled commands.
findings.title: Avoid building a shell command from userName

findings.body: `toBeTruthy()` does not verify that `renderReport` preserves the input rows, so this test would still pass if the function dropped or reordered data. The test should assert the exact expected array to protect the requirement.
findings.title: Assert the returned rows, not just truthiness

findings.body: Building a shell command string and passing it through `sh -c` makes `user` part of the shell parse rather than a plain argument. Any spaces or shell metacharacters in the username can change the command that runs, which is a command-injection risk compared to the previous `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` call.
findings.failure_scenario: A username like `alice; rm -rf /` is interpolated into the shell command, causing `sh` to execute unintended commands instead of just passing the username to `report`.
findings.title: Avoid invoking the shell with interpolated user input

findings.body: `skip(1)` unconditionally removes the first row from every report, so the function no longer preserves the input rows. This changes the returned data for all non-empty reports and contradicts the stated behavior of preserving report rows for named users.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains `["first", "second"]`, the function now returns only `"second"`, causing callers to lose the first report row.
findings.title: Keep all report rows instead of dropping the first one

findings.body: Building a shell command with `format!("report --user {user}")` and passing it to `sh -c` makes `user` shell-interpreted. A crafted name can inject additional commands, and even benign names with spaces or metacharacters will be parsed differently than the previous direct `Command::new("report")` call.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller passes `alice; rm -rf /` as the user, `sh -c` executes both `report` and the injected command instead of just invoking the report binary.
findings.title: Avoid invoking the shell with interpolated user input

findings.body: This validates the resolved path and then opens it in a separate step, so an attacker who can mutate the filesystem between `canonicalize()` and `File::open()` can swap the checked file for a different target and bypass the prefix check. For a path-access control boundary, the check and open need to happen atomically (for example via a directory fd / `openat`-style API or a no-follow open on the already-validated directory).
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker can race a symlink or rename inside `root`, they can get `File::open(candidate)` to open an unintended file after the prefix check has already passed, resulting in arbitrary file reads.

findings.body: Interpolating `user` into a `sh -c` command turns the argument into shell input instead of a normal process argument. Any username containing shell metacharacters can alter the executed command, which is both a correctness and security regression compared with the previous direct `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` call.
findings.failure_scenario: A username like `alice; rm -rf /` is passed in, the shell executes the extra command, and the report process runs with attacker-controlled arguments.
findings.title: Avoid invoking the report command through a shell

findings.body: Slicing the result with `sublist(1)` discards the first row for every non-empty input and throws on an empty list. That changes the function from a passthrough into one that loses data and can fail on valid inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is empty, `sublist(1)` raises a `RangeError`; when `rows` contains data, the first row is silently dropped, so callers receive incomplete reports.
findings.title: Return the full row list instead of dropping the first entry

findings.body: This changes the process invocation from a direct argv call to `sh -c`, so the user name is now interpolated into a shell command. That contradicts the requirement to pass user names as arguments without a shell and also opens the door to shell metacharacter interpretation if `user` contains unexpected characters.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name like `alice; rm -rf /` is interpolated into the shell command, so the spawned shell executes more than the intended report command instead of treating the name as a single argument.
findings.title: Pass the user argument directly instead of invoking a shell

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: `isNotNull` does not verify the behavior that changed in `renderReport`, so this test would still pass if the function truncated rows or returned the wrong contents. A regression test should check the exact list produced by the call.
findings.failure_scenario: If `renderReport` starts dropping rows or returning the wrong values again, this test still passes and the bug ships unnoticed.
findings.title: Assert the returned rows instead of only non-nullness

findings.body: Passing `user` through `/bin/sh -c` turns it into a shell command string, so values containing spaces or shell metacharacters can change the executed command. The previous `ProcessBuilder` call treated the user value as a single argument instead of code to be interpreted by a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: If a named user contains shell syntax such as `alice; rm -rf /`, the spawned process executes the extra shell fragment instead of running `report` with that username.
findings.title: Avoid invoking the shell with unescaped user input

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` removes the first element from every result set, which contradicts the stated intent to preserve report rows and also throws on empty input because the start index is greater than the end index.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains `first, second`, the method returns only `second`; when `rows` is empty, `subList(1, 0)` throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the report rows unchanged.
findings.title: Return the full row list instead of dropping the first entry

findings.body: This test no longer verifies the method's observable output, so it would pass even if `render` drops rows or returns the wrong list contents.
findings.failure_scenario: If `render` starts removing elements or returning the wrong data, the test still passes because any non-null list satisfies `assertNotNull`.
findings.title: Assert the returned rows, not just non-nullity

findings.body: Passing `user` through `sh -c` concatenates it into a shell command, so any metacharacters in the username are interpreted by the shell instead of being treated as data. If `user` comes from an external caller, this allows command injection when `Render` runs.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username like `alice; rm -rf /`, and `sh -c` executes the injected command after `report --user`, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid shell command injection in Render

findings.body: `rows[1:]` panics when `rows` is empty and silently discards the first element for every non-empty input. The previous implementation returned the original slice unchanged, so this alters behavior and introduces a crash path.
findings.failure_scenario: If `Render` is called with an empty slice, the new slice expression panics; if it is called with one or more rows, the first row is always removed, which changes the returned report data.
findings.title: Guard the slice before dropping the first row

findings.body: The new test only asserts that Render does not return nil, which would still pass if the function drops rows. That weakens coverage for the spec requirement that rendering preserves every row.
findings.title: Restore a test that checks row preservation

findings.body: Switching this workflow to `pull_request_target` makes it run in the base repository context, and the added checkout of `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` executes attacker-controlled PR code while repository secrets are available to later steps. That allows a forked PR to reach privileged workflow context instead of the unprivileged `pull_request` context.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a PR from a fork; the workflow checks out the PR head and later runs its code under `pull_request_target`, so any malicious changes in the PR can access repo-scoped credentials and affect the base repository.
findings.title: Avoid running untrusted pull request code in pull_request_target

findings.body: Passing `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN` into `npm test` makes the token available to whatever test or lifecycle scripts the PR controls. In combination with checking out the PR head, a malicious PR can read and exfiltrate that secret during the test run.
findings.failure_scenario: If a forked PR adds code that prints environment variables or runs a postinstall/test hook, `npm test` will leak `RELEASE_TOKEN` to the attacker and compromise the release credential.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN to npm test

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret
